indicators.note: breaking the words up lets their letters be put back together in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that hard men are the sort who crack ribs, and another agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' looks like what the tough guys do, but it tells you to rearrange RIBS SURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Bruisers are big, aggressive men who like a fight, a synonym for tough guys.

clue.text: Initiation that's suitable is in British Museum

indicators.note: in tells you the following pieces sit inside the abbreviation for the museum

parts.note: BM is the standard abbreviation for the British Museum in London
apt means suitable or fitting

explanation.surface: A fitting ceremony of initiation, it seems, is held at the British Museum.
explanation.walkthrough: BM is a crossword staple for the British Museum in London; 'that's' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Baptism is the Christian rite of admission into the church, so a ceremony of initiation.

clue.text: Family member doesn't start to let loose

indicators.note: a word that doesn't start has lost its opening letter

parts.note: an auntie is a family member, a parent's sister

explanation.surface: A relative isn't the one to begin releasing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't start' removes the A from AUNTIE.
explanation.definitionFit: To untie a knot or a rope is to unfasten it and so set something free.

clue.text: Jump on places for putting veg

parts.note: to spring is to jump
greens are the smooth areas of a golf course where players putt

explanation.surface: A golfer leaps onto the greens where vegetables seem to have been planted.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means the first word sits on top of the second. Spring greens are young cabbage leaves, a common British vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Spring greens are early, loose-leaved cabbages eaten as a green vegetable.

clue.text: Province in actual centre of Germany

parts.note: real means actual or genuine

indicators.note: the centre of a seven-letter word is its fourth letter

explanation.surface: A region situated right in the heart of Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm is a kingdom or domain, and figuratively a field of activity, like a province.

clue.text: Like one with a large landmass

parts.note: as means like, in the way of
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Something compared to a person who owns a great deal of land.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is the biggest continent, the largest single expanse of land on Earth.

definitions.meaning: to pull out of a race or contest
a small graze or cut on the skin

explanation.surface: An athlete pulls out of an event because of a small knock.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are common: a horse is scratched from a race, and a scratch is a slight wound.

indicators.note: almost means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: the adder is Britain's only venomous snake
d is the standard abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: An additional serpent very nearly perished.
explanation.definitionFit: Something added is additional or extra, put in on top of what was there.

clue.text: Simple dish — not as snob ate in mess

indicators.note: a mess of these letters is a jumbled version of them

explanation.surface: A plain meal that a snobbish diner would never eat in the officers' mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess' looks like the military canteen, but it signals rearranging NOT AS SNOB ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Beans on toast is a cheap, basic British meal of baked beans served on toasted bread.

indicators.note: follows tells you the Queen's letters come after the favourite's

parts.note: a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: The monarch comes after her preferred holy man.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Peter was the apostle traditionally seen as the first Pope.

clue.text: A word we hear in a German accent? So it's alleged

indicators.text: we hear in a German accent
indicators.note: we hear points to how the words sound, said the way a stage German would say them, with V for W

parts.note: said as a German stereotype might, 'a word' comes out with a V and a rolled R

explanation.surface: A jokey question about how a German speaker pronounces a word, ending with something claimed.
explanation.walkthrough: The comic stage German turns W into V, so 'a word' becomes 'a verred'.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to state firmly; averred means asserted or declared, close to alleged.

indicators.note: inside places the cold letter within the abbreviation

parts.note: ie is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A cool box, that is, one with cold air inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice is put in drinks or boxes to chill them, so it acts as a coolant.

indicators.note: to change these letters is to arrange them differently

explanation.surface: Someone insists they won't alter the name put forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' looks like the refusal, but it asks you to rearrange NAME I DONT.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate who is nominated has been put forward or proposed for a role.

clue.text: I'm taken aback by anger? That's an illusion

indicators.note: taken aback, read literally, means turned back to front

parts.note: rage is fierce anger

explanation.surface: Someone startled by their own fury wonders if they imagined it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken aback' looks like surprise, but read literally it means turned backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion, such as water seen shimmering in a desert.

clue.text: Cock Robin initially waving to Rose

indicators.note: initially picks the opening letter of the bird's name
waving suggests the letters moving about into a new order

explanation.surface: Cock Robin, the nursery-rhyme bird, first greets someone named Rose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waving' rearranges TO ROSE into OOSTER, after R from Robin.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster is a male domestic fowl, the cock of the farmyard.

indicators.note: ignoring the second means leaving out the word's second letter

parts.note: a brother is a sibling

explanation.surface: A sibling who pays no attention to the runner-up makes a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring the second' drops the second letter R from BROTHER.
explanation.definitionFit: Bother means trouble or fuss, a minor disturbance, as in 'a spot of bother'.

definitions.meaning: to abstain from something, keep oneself from doing it
the repeated lines sung after each verse of a song

explanation.surface: A singer is told to stay quiet during the sung chorus.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb sense is to abstain; the noun sense is the lines repeated after each verse.

clue.text: Lorna's family has least amount of data to contribute

parts.note: Lorna Doone, heroine of R D Blackmore's novel, belongs to the outlaw Doone family of Exmoor
a bit is the smallest unit of computer data

explanation.surface: A literary heroine's clan provides the barest scrap of information.
explanation.walkthrough: Lorna Doone is an 1869 English novel; her family are the Doones, so 'Lorna's family has' reads DOONES.
explanation.definitionFit: To do one's bit is an idiom meaning to make one's own contribution to a shared effort.

indicators.note: extremely, read as at the extremes, picks the word's outer letters

parts.note: pot is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: A very attractive pharmacy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for desirable, but it takes its ends, D and E.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is a warehouse or storehouse where goods or vehicles are kept.

definitions.meaning: a cheer of approval, like 'well done!'
in the NATO phonetic alphabet the word before Charlie stands for B

explanation.surface: Someone cheers on Charlie's forerunner in a job.
explanation.walkthrough: In the radio alphabet Alpha, Bravo, Charlie stand for A, B, C, so Bravo comes just before Charlie.
explanation.definitionFit: Shouted at a performance it means well done; in the phonetic alphabet it is the code word for B.

indicators.note: seen in says the letters can be spotted within the following words

explanation.surface: A fairy has been spotted in a hotel lobby.
explanation.definitionFit: An elf is a small mischievous fairy, the same kind of creature as a sprite.

clue.text: Uncommon sense in a German city

indicators.note: uncommon, read as not in its usual form, asks for the letters reordered

explanation.surface: Rare good judgement found in a German town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncommon' looks like a description of the sense, but it rearranges SENSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr region of western Germany.

indicators.note: awkward suggests the letters are put together clumsily, in a different order

explanation.surface: A gardener struggles to stake an unwieldy bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: The petunia is a popular trumpet-shaped garden flower grown in beds and baskets.

definitions.meaning: on a ship out on the ocean

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about a muddled sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone bewildered; literally it means being out on the ocean.

indicators.note: beside places the Mormon's last letter next to the sailor, here following it

parts.note: a salt, or old salt, is a sailor, as is a tar

indicators.note: end picks the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A Mormon finishes his journey next to the Great Salt Lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'salt lake' suggests Salt Lake City, home of the Mormons, but 'salt' is a sailor, TAR, and 'lake' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarn is a small mountain lake, a word used especially in northern England.

clue.text: Begin to understand material one doesn't finish

parts.note: cotton is a fabric

indicators.note: doesn't finish means the word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A dressmaker starts to grasp a fabric they never complete.
explanation.definitionFit: To cotton on is a colloquial idiom meaning to grasp or realise something at last.
